entries.definition: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal.
entries.example: Sodium loses one electron to chlorine: Na becomes Na⁺, Cl becomes Cl⁻, and the opposite charges attract to form NaCl.

entries.definition: An atom or group of atoms with a charge, formed by losing or gaining electrons. Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain them to form negative ions.
entries.example: A metal M forming M³⁺ needs three O²⁻ for every two M³⁺ to balance the charge, giving $\text{M}_2\text{O}_3$.

entries.definition: The regular three-dimensional arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions in an ionic compound, held by strong forces in every direction.
entries.example: Sodium chloride has a cubic lattice. Its high melting point comes from the many strong attractions that must all be broken.

entries.definition: Ionic compounds do not conduct as solids because the ions are fixed in the lattice, but they do when molten or dissolved, because the ions are then free to move and carry charge.
entries.example: Solid NaCl does not conduct; molten NaCl and salt water both do. The rule to state is *the ions are free to move*.

entries.definition: A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms, held by the attraction of both nuclei to the shared pair.
entries.example: In O₂ each oxygen needs two more electrons, so they share **two** pairs: a double bond. In N₂ they share three pairs.

entries.definition: A drawing showing which atom each bonding electron came from, using dots for one atom and crosses for the other. It shows the electrons but not the shape, sizes or real distances.
entries.example: In HCl a single dot-and-cross pair sits between the two atoms; the outer shell of Cl is drawn with its other six electrons as three lone pairs.

entries.definition: A pair of outer electrons not involved in bonding.
entries.example: In water the oxygen has two bonding pairs, to the hydrogens, and two lone pairs, which is why the molecule is bent rather than straight.

entries.definition: Substances made of small molecules with strong covalent bonds **inside** each molecule but weak intermolecular forces **between** them, so they melt and boil at low temperatures.
entries.example: Water, carbon dioxide and methane. Boiling water breaks the weak forces between molecules, not the O–H bonds inside them.

entries.definition: The weak attractions **between** molecules, far weaker than the covalent bonds inside them. They get stronger as molecules get larger, which is why bigger molecules boil at higher temperatures.
entries.example: Poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature because its molecules are very long, so the total intermolecular force is large even though each contact is weak.

entries.definition: A structure where every atom is joined by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network, so melting it means breaking covalent bonds: very high melting points.
entries.example: Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide. Diamond's carbon atoms each bond to four others in a rigid 3D lattice, which is why it is so hard.

entries.definition: A giant covalent form of carbon in which every atom bonds to four others in a rigid three-dimensional lattice. Very hard, very high melting point, and does not conduct electricity because there are no free electrons.
entries.example: Used in cutting tools. All four outer electrons of each carbon are in bonds, so none is free to carry charge.

entries.definition: A form of carbon where each atom bonds to only three others in flat layers, leaving one delocalised electron per atom. The layers slide, so it is soft, and the free electrons make it conduct.
entries.example: Pencil lead and electrodes. Same element as diamond, opposite properties, because of the number of bonds per atom.

entries.definition: A single layer of graphite, one atom thick. Very strong for its mass and an excellent conductor, because of the delocalised electrons.
entries.example: A sheet of graphene one atom thick is about 200 times stronger than steel by weight, and is being developed for electronics and composites.

entries.definition: A molecule of carbon atoms arranged in a hollow ball or tube, with rings of five, six or seven atoms. Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, is the best known.
entries.example: C₆₀ is a hollow sphere like a football. Carbon **nanotubes** are cylindrical fullerenes with a very high length-to-diameter ratio and high tensile strength.

entries.definition: A particle between 1 and 100 nm across, containing only a few hundred atoms. Their huge surface area to volume ratio makes them behave differently from the bulk material.
entries.example: For a cube of side $s$ the ratio is $\dfrac{6s^2}{s^3} = \dfrac{6}{s}$. Dropping from 10 nm to 2 nm raises it from 0.6 to 3 per nm, five times more.

entries.definition: Total surface area divided by volume. It rises as an object gets smaller, which is why nanoparticles make such effective catalysts: far more of their atoms are on the surface.
entries.example: A 2 nm cube has a ratio of 3 per nm against 0.6 for a 10 nm cube, so a given mass of the smaller particles offers five times the reacting surface.

entries.definition: A lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. The attraction between the ions and those electrons is the bond, and it acts in every direction.
entries.example: In copper, each atom donates its outer electrons to the sea. The strong attraction gives a high melting point, and the free electrons carry charge and heat.

entries.definition: Electrons not held by any one atom, free to move through the whole structure. They are what makes metals and graphite conduct electricity and heat.
entries.example: In a metal wire the delocalised electrons drift when a voltage is applied, carrying the current. Graphite has one per atom for the same reason.

entries.definition: Able to be hammered or rolled into shape without breaking. Pure metals are malleable because their layers of identical ions can slide over each other.
entries.example: Copper is rolled into sheet and drawn into wire. Alloying it disrupts the layers and makes it harder, which is the trade-off.

entries.definition: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. The different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers so they cannot slide easily, which makes an alloy harder than the pure metal.
entries.example: Steel is iron with carbon; bronze is copper with tin. Both are harder than the pure metal they are based on, for exactly that reason.

entries.definition: A very long molecule made by joining many small molecules together. Its molecules are large, so the intermolecular forces add up to a lot and polymers are solid at room temperature.
entries.example: Poly(ethene) is made from many ethene molecules. Strong covalent bonds run along the chain; the weaker forces between chains still hold it solid.

entries.definition: The pull between opposite charges. It is the reason behind ionic bonds, metallic bonds and the attraction of nuclei to a shared pair in a covalent bond.
entries.example: In NaCl the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions attract; in copper the positive ions attract the electron sea. Naming the charges involved is what earns the mark.

entries.definition: Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.
entries.example: Diamond, graphite, graphene and the fullerenes are all allotropes of carbon; their very different properties come from how the atoms are joined, not from what they are.
